Paragraph: Overwhelmed by blinding grief and suppressed rage after the total annihilation of his hundred sons, the blind king Dhritarashtra arrived at the battlefield of Kurukshetra alongside Gandhari. When the victorious Pandavas came forward to seek his blessings, Dhritarashtra embraced Yudhishthira with forced composure, but his heart burned with intense vengefulness toward Bhima—the slayer of Duryodhana and his brothers. Demanding to embrace Bhima, his intent was to crush the prince to death within his formidable arms. Realizing the danger, Krishna silently pushed an iron statue of Bhima forward in his place. Harnessing all his physical strength and violent anguish, Dhritarashtra shattered the metal statue into pieces, vomiting blood from the extreme exertion. When his rage suddenly collapsed into profound horror and weeping regret over his perceived fratricide, Krishna revealed the deception, urging the king to process his grief without succumbing to murderous malice.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Dhritarashtra experiences an extreme surge of bereavement-fueled fury and displacement of blame, attempting to murder Bhima under the guise of an affectionate embrace to compensate for his overwhelming sense of loss and helplessness.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Dhritarashtra surrenders to violent impulses as an outlet for unprocessed grief, but upon believing he succeeded, he immediately suffers intense remorse, enabling Krishna to intervene with cognitive reframing about his responsibility in the disaster.
Outcome/Resolution: The destruction of the iron statue dissipates Dhritarashtra's physical rage, allowing him to acknowledge his grief authentically and extend peace to the Pandavas.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Stress Management: Extreme Distress Tolerance Deficit, Acute Emotional Overload
Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Fear: Existential Void, Terror of Absolute Loss
Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Anger Management: Displaced Aggression, Murderous Rage, Impulse Control Collapse

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Putra-Shoka (The catastrophic, debilitating grief resulting from the loss of one's children)
Vaira (Deeply ingrained enmity and vengefulness corrupting moral judgment)
Moha-Avrita (Mind completely shrouded by delusion and toxic attachment)
पश्चात्ताप / Paschattapa (Immediate burning remorse following impulsive destructive action)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Dhritarashtra's attempt to crush Bhima illustrates how 'Moha' (blind attachment) converts profound loss into 'Vaira' (malice). His physical breakdown over the iron statue signifies how ego-driven revenge destroys the perpetrator's own vitality without curing spiritual grief ('Putra-Shoka').
Brief_Summary_Psychological: This passage highlights severe trauma projection, cathartic breakdown, and displaced aggression. Unable to process his own complicity in his sons' downfall, Dhritarashtra projects all grief into murderous rage toward Bhima; the destruction of the surrogate object (statue) acts as a violent psychological release that forces him to confront his underlying remorse.
